claims.text: Oxidation resistance and material integrity are governed by formation of a stable nanoscale oxide layer.
The stable nanoscale oxide layer acts as a barrier to further oxidation and degradation.
The proposed initial material is a polycrystalline multiprincipal-element alloy with uniform composition and microstructure.
Oxide formation and evolution will be characterized using in-situ TEM and atom probe tomography.
The hypothesized protective oxide layer has a thickness of 10-50 nm.
Oxide formation and growth involve atomic diffusion.
Oxide formation involves nucleation and growth of oxide precipitates.
The stable oxide layer will reduce oxidation rate by 30% relative to the baseline.
The stable oxide layer will improve material integrity by 25% relative to the baseline.
Material integrity will be assessed through oxide-layer thickness and alloy lifespan.
The baseline is a conventional alloy having a non-stable oxide layer.
The hypothesis is proposed to hold from 800°C to 1000°C and oxygen partial pressures from 10^-5 to 10^-3 atm.
A controlled comparison of multiprincipal-element alloys with and without a stable oxide layer is proposed.
Failure to reduce oxidation rate by at least 20% and to improve material integrity by at least 15% relative to baseline is specified as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The baseline is defined as a conventional alloy, whereas the experimental design describes comparison between multiprincipal-element alloys with and without the stable oxide layer. These are not clearly the same control.
